analysis.one_liner: Requires safer design, retrofit, and phase-out of rail tank cars hauling crude oil and flammable liquids.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced by one Democrat with 8 Democratic cosponsors, died in House committee without a hearing or a vote.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have directed the Transportation Department to write tougher design rules for the DOT-111 tank cars that haul crude oil and other flammable liquids — steel jackets, thermal protection, shields, and better pressure valves — and required upgrades to newer cars, plus a plan to phase out older cars that were never upgraded. It also would have required crude oil tank cars to be watched, never left unattended, during transfers between railroads or between a railroad and a shipper. It was referred to two House committees in April 2015 and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: People who live and work along the rail lines that carry crude oil — residents of towns the trains pass through, rail workers, and firefighters who respond to derailments — would face a lower risk of fires, spills, and explosions from punctured or ruptured cars. Tank car manufacturers would also gain orders for new, safer cars.

how_it_helps.text: Requires the Transportation Department to write stronger design standards for new tank cars — an outer steel jacket, thermal protection, full-height head shields, and high-flow pressure relief valves — the features that keep a car from tearing open in a derailment.

Requires safety upgrades to tank cars built after October 2011, including high-flow relief valves and design changes that keep bottom outlets from opening in a crash, cutting the chance of a slow, hard-to-detect spill.

Requires a Homeland Security rule that no tank car carrying crude oil ever be left unattended while being transferred between railroads or between a railroad and a shipper, closing a security and spill-risk gap during the handoff.
Directs the Transportation Secretary to send Congress a plan to phase out, 'on an aggressive basis,' older DOT-111 cars that are not retrofitted — the least protective cars in the fleet.

analysis.who_pays: Crude oil shippers, freight railroads, and tank car owners would pay for new safer cars, retrofits, and added security procedures during transfers. Some of those costs would likely be passed through in shipping charges and, in turn, energy prices.
analysis.who_pays_short: Oil shippers, railroads, and tank car owners

drawbacks.text: The retrofit and phase-out mandates would impose substantial upgrade costs on shippers, railroads, and tank car owners for cars already in service, and those costs could be passed on to consumers through shipping and energy prices.
The security provision would add operational burdens — crews or monitoring for every crude oil transfer between carriers — on railroads and shippers, with no funding attached to the mandate.
The bill set a one-year deadline for new rules but appropriated no money for enforcement or inspection, leaving the agencies to absorb the workload.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The safety benefits would land on specific communities — the towns along crude-oil routes and the crews and first responders near any derailment — while the costs would be spread across shippers and railroads and passed through modestly to consumers, a trade most safety regulation accepts. An honest supporter would also acknowledge that the Department of Transportation was already finalizing its own tank car rule in 2015 with similar design requirements, so the bill's incremental gain over that rulemaking was limited, and its one-year deadlines were aggressive and unfunded. The bill's real value would have been writing the standards into statute so they could not be loosened later.

outcome.mechanism: The bill was sent to two House committees and their subcommittees in April 2015 and never got a hearing, a markup, or a floor vote before the 114th Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Donald Payne Jr. introduced the bill on April 14, 2015, joined by eight Democratic cosponsors, to mandate tougher design standards and a phase-out for the DOT-111 tank cars that haul crude oil and other flammable liquids.

The House referred it to the Transportation and Infrastructure Committee and the Homeland Security Committee the same day, and within three days it was further split between the Subcommittee on Railroads, Pipelines, and Hazardous Materials and the Subcommittee on Transportation Security.
No further action was ever recorded — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill died when the 114th Congress ended on January 3, 2017.

The practical effect was blunted because the Transportation Department issued its own tank car rule in 2015 requiring similar upgrades, so the industry faced binding requirements from a regulation rather than from a law Congress could not easily weaken.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Oil shippers, railroads, and tank car owners avoided new statutory retrofit and phase-out deadlines. In practice they were not off the hook — DOT's separate 2015 rule imposed similar requirements — but the requirements rested on a regulation that future administrations could revise rather than on a law.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Oil shippers, railroads, and tank car owners

sides.party_line_note: All nine supporters — the sponsor and eight cosponsors — were Democrats, no Republican ever signed on, and the Republican-chaired committees never brought the bill up, though no vote was ever taken to confirm the split.

industries.note: Shippers would bear the cost of moving their oil only in cars meeting the new design standards, retrofitting newer cars, and phasing out un-retrofitted older ones. Those costs are the direct price of reducing fire and spill risk to the towns the trains pass through.

Railroads would pay for upgrades and for the new requirement that crude oil cars never be left unattended during transfers, but safer cars also mean fewer derailments, fires, and liability claims on their own networks.

industries.industry: Tank car manufacturers and leasing companies
industries.note: Builders would gain orders for jacketed, better-protected new cars, while owners and lessors of the existing fleet would eat retrofit and early-retirement costs on cars they had already paid for.
